Instant petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C is at the behest of the petitioner for quashing of the FIR and the criminal proceeding in connection with G.R. Case No.745 of 2022 pending in the file of learned J.M.F.C.(O), Bhubaneswar corresponding to Nandankanan P.S. Case No. 0093 of 2022 arising out of 1.C.C. Case No. 3588 of 2022, on the grounds inter alia that the criminal prosecution initiated against him is untenable in law and hence, therefore, it is liable to be interfered with.
2.

Briefly stated, the informant, namely, opposite party No.2 filed the complaint in 1.C.C Case No.
3588 of 2022 before the learned court below, wherein, by order dated 13th June, 2022, the local police was directed to register a case, consequent upon which, Nandankanan P.S. Case No.0093 dated 30th June, 2022 was registered under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 384, 385 and 506 I.P.C.

The challenge is with regard to the criminal proceeding as a whole, which has been set into motion,
after Nandankanan P.S. Case No.0093 of 2022 was registered.

The principal ground of challenge is that the petitioner had an agreement with opposite party No.2 to supply land and the same is a dispute pursuant to a Sameer Pattnaik Vrs. State of Odisha & Another contract between the parties as per a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) executed on 15th September, 2020.

3. Heard Mr. Sidhartha Mishra, learned counsel for the petitioner and Mr. A.K. Budhia, learned counsel for opposite party No.2 besides learned counsel for the State-opposite party No.1.
4.

Mr. Mishra, learned counsel for the petitioner submits that there has been no fraud committed by the petitioner so to say and he acted in accordance with the contract later to the execution of MoU dated 15th September, 2020.

It is further submitted that both the parties entered into an agreement as per the MoU, out of forty (40) plots measuring an area of Ac.06.156 decimal, land with an area of Ac.2.0730 decimal has been sold to opposite party No.2 and there has been payments made in that regard with an outstanding due of Rs.6,17,05,613/-(Rupees Six Crore Seventeen Lakh Five Thousand Six Hundred Thirteen) payable which has not been received by the petitioner till date as per the MoU.

Furthermore, the allegations in the complaint are outrightly false and fabricated and an imaginary story created by the informant (complainant), as a result of which, Nandankanan P.S.
Case No. 0093 of 2022 has been registered.

It is contended that considering the nature of dispute and the fact that parties Sameer Pattnaik Vrs. State of Odisha & Another entered into a contract,
continuation of the criminal prosecution would be an abuse of process of law and hence, therefore, it should be quashed in exercise of the Court's inherent jurisdiction.

sentences.text: 5. Learned counsel for the State-opposite party No.1 submits that since the case has been registered and the allegation is to the effect that the petitioner committed certain mischief while dealing with the opposite party No.2, law is to take its own course.

Mr. Budhia, learned counsel for opposite party No.2 submitted that considering the nature of allegation against the petitioner as to cheating and fraud, investigation is underway, which is pursuant to the direction of the learned Court below exercising its jurisdiction under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C and in such view of the matter, extra-ordinary jurisdiction should not be exercised to quash the criminal prosecution, when the investigation is still on.

While contending so, Mr. Budhia cited a decision of the Apex Court in Minu Kumari Vrs. State of Bihar reported in 2006 (7) SRJ 235, which is with regard to the powers to be exercised under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

2043 instituted by its land owner to declare the sale deed as null and void to be pending, the fact which was never disclosed by the petitioner.
6.

It has been informed to the Court as to the conduct of the petitioner for having committed mischief earlier for which not less than eight (8) F.I.Rs have been lodged against him in different Police Stations, details of which have been disclosed and while making such disclosures, Mr. Budhia,
learned counsel for the opposite party No.2 submits that it was beyond reasonable doubt that the petitioner to be a habitual offender and has indulged himself in tampering documents for which criminal cases have been registered against him with the allegation of cheating.

Under such circumstances, Mr. Budhia, learned counsel for the opposite party No.2 submits that the jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should not be exercised to scuttle the investigation which is at its inception and also not permitted in law in view of the decision in Ch. Bhajan Lal (Supra).
7. No doubt, there has been a contract between the parties.
In that connection, an MoU was executed in 2020.
As per the MoU, the petitioner was required to provide litigation free lands to opposite party No.2.

There is no dispute over the fact that in connection with the contract, the petitioner received the consideration amount from opposite party No.2, who runs the company,
namely, M/s. Evos Buildcon Pvt. Ltd.
The payments Sameer Pattnaik Vrs. State of Odisha & Another have been received by the petitioner on number of occasions and principally through Bank transfers which is also not in question.

However, the allegation in the complaint (FIR) is that the petitioner though had agreed upon to provide and selling of lands free of litigation, some of the transactions, however, found to be no so as the land owners challenged such claim of the petitioner by placing one of the instances, where the suit in C.S. No. 2043 of 2023 was instituted by a land owner on the ground of having obtained the sale deed by fraud.
The details of the criminal cases pending against the petitioner have also been drawn to the attention of the Court by Mr. Budhia.

The circumstances leading to the filing of the complaint and thereafter registration of Nandankanan P.S. Case No. 0093 of 2022 have been described by opposite party No.2 in the complaint, a copy of which is at Annexure-1.
The allegation against the petitioner is that he cheated and by fraudulent means alienated the lands claiming it to be free of litigation and all encumbrances.

It is alleged that the terms and conditions of the MoU have been violated and not only that by cheating and misrepresentation, the petitioner managed to receive an amount of Rs.6,33,00,000/- (Rupees Six Crore Thirty Three Lakh) from the company.
In other words, the petitioner is alleged to have not supplied litigation free lands which was the understanding between him and opposite party No.2.

It is further alleged that when opposite party No.2 wanted to take possession of the lands, it was seriously objected to by some of the land owners even by 3rd Party/Strangers/ litigants and also placed on record about one of such cases in which the land owner even declined to acknowledge the petitioner.

With such allegation, the complaint was filed by opposite party No.2, who is the purchaser of the lands allegedly Sameer Pattnaik Vrs. State of Odisha & Another managed through the petitioner who said to be an agent/broker and in that connection, huge amount of money has been paid and received between the parties.

The question is,

Mr. Mishra, learned counsel for the petitioner, as it is made to appear from his argument, there has been no fraud and the transactions are pursuant to the MoU between the parties and therefore,
the criminal prosecution has been unnecessarily thrust upon the petitioner which is thus required to be quashed.

It is the contention that the dispute is civil in nature and it was in respect of a contract between the petitioner and opposite party No.2 and in absence of any such fraud having been committed, the criminal proceeding as against the petitioner would be an abuse of process of law.

In response to above, Mr. Budhia, learned counsel for opposite party No.2 claims that there has been misrepresentation as well as fraud since the petitioner persuaded opposite party No.2 to enter into a contract when the lands some of which were not litigation free.

sentences.text: The decision in Ch. Bhajan Lal (Supra) laid down the principles and legal position as to the circumstances where inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. may be exercised.

According to the said decision, where the FIR or complaint, even if they are taken at its face value and accepted in entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or a case against the accused; or where, it does not disclose a cognizable offence to have been committed: or where the uncontroverted allegations therein and the evidence is collected in support thereof do not disclose any such commission of offence, jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. shall have to be exercised in order to do complete justice.

The Apex Court also held in the aforesaid decision that if the F.I.R. or Complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused or that the criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with malafide or instituted maliciously with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge,
in such circumstances as well, power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. may be exercised.

Applying the above set of norms laid down by the Apex Court, the Court has to consider, if a case prima facie is made against the petitioner or not considering the complaint (FIR).
10.
Inherent jurisdiction Section 482 Cr.P.C. is not fettered with any limitation.
Such power is extra-ordinary to meet situations and circumstances with a purpose to do justice in a given case.

If no prima facie case is made out even by a plain reading of FIR or Complaint as the case may be or no cognizable offence is made to appear and committed, such jurisdiction may be exercised in order to advance the cause of justice.

While exercising inherent jurisdiction, the Court is also to bear in mind the limitation and not to stifle investigation or criminal prosecution, especially when Sameer Sameer Pattnaik vs State Of Odisha & Another ....

Pattnaik Vrs. State of Odisha & Another disputed questions of fact are involved.
The Court is not to hold a roving inquiry into the allegations of F.I.R. or Complaint and to reach at a conclusion one way or other and whether, it would result in conviction or not.

It has the duty to examine and go through the contents of the F.I.R. and evidence received for the purpose and to consider whether a prima face case is proved and if not made out to exercise the jurisdiction of Section 482 Cr.P.C.
11.
As to the present case, the F.I.R. was lodged later to the direction received from the learned Court below under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.
The investigation is in progress as earlier stated.
The allegation of cheating is made against the petitioner.
The petitioner is also alleged of false representation suppressing the facts with regard to litigations in respect of couple of transactions.
The specific instances of such misrepresentation stand narrated in the complaint.
In such view of the matter, the allegation of opposite party no.2 in the F.I.R. is needed to be examined during investigation.
The outcome of investigation would reveal whether there was any mischief or fraud committed by the petitioner at the time of entering into the contract and in the process of selling of lands.

12. As to if there is no fraud or any kind of misrepresentation by the petitioner or whether it is pure and simple a contract between the parties and hence the dispute to be civil in nature, an argument which is advanced by Mr. Mishra, learned counsel appearing for him would be a matter of examination only after collection of evidence and in case the investigation results in submission of chargesheet.

In other words, it would be too premature to accept any such contention that the dispute to be civil in nature particularly when the investigation is at its nascent stage and the complaint is with the allegation of cheating and false representation or fraud committed by the petitioner.
Sameer Pattnaik Vrs. State of Odisha & Another 13.

14. Accordingly, it is ordered.
15. In the result, the CRLMC stands dismissed.
